script.opening: "Afternoon. So my wife’s been on at me about a mole on my back — says it’s got bigger and looks a bit different. Honestly I think she’s fussing; I’ve got loads of moles, I’m outside all day, they all change a bit don’t they. I’ve taken a photo if that helps. I really just want you to tell me it’s nothing so she’ll stop worrying, then I can get back to the job."

facts.text: If characterised (history + photo): CHANGE over ~4 months — grown in size, now asymmetric with an irregular border, two or three colours (light/dark brown, black), ~8 mm diameter, intermittent itch, and one episode of minor bleeding. This change-plus-irregularity is the suspicious picture; several 7-point-checklist features are present.

On questioning: lifelong outdoor occupation (roofer) with chronic and intermittent intense UV exposure, fair skin that burns, multiple childhood/adult sunburns, never uses sun protection, multiple moles. High melanoma risk profile.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "it’s nothing, she’s fussing" is bravado over fear: a workmate died of melanoma that "spread everywhere" a couple of years ago, and Keith is privately frightened it could be the same, but as the family’s sole earner he can’t face the idea of being ill or off work, so he minimises. Booking a video and pushing for reassurance is avoidance. The wife’s concern is the reliable signal.
If reached: self-employed, no sick pay, mortgage, kids; the thought of cancer is also the thought of not providing. He jokes to cover real dread, and there’s guilt about years of ignoring sun safety.

Officially: quick reassurance to placate his wife. What he needs: in-person examination of the lesion (and the rest of his skin), recognition that a changing, irregular pigmented lesion warrants a melanoma suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12: weighted 7-point checklist score of 3 or more — his is about 9), sun-safety advice without shaming, and his fear addressed.

ice.ideas: It’s just one of his many moles; they all change a bit; his wife is fussing.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a workmate died of melanoma that spread; he’s privately frightened it’s the same but, as sole earner, can’t face being ill, so he minimises; guilt about years of no sun protection.
ice.expectations: Quick reassurance it’s nothing. What he actually needs: examination and a melanoma suspected cancer pathway referral for a changing irregular lesion, with sun-safety advice and his fear addressed.

cues: Changing + irregular + multi-coloured + itch/bleed pigmented lesion — suspicious; don’t reassure from a glance/photo.
"They all change, she’s fussing" — minimising; the wife’s concern is the reliable signal and the fear is underneath.
Outdoor worker, fair skin, repeated sunburns — a high-risk melanoma profile.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a CHANGING, irregular, multi-coloured pigmented lesion (with itch/bleeding) as suspicious for melanoma, and does NOT reassure it away from a photo/glance or accept "they all change"

Applies structured assessment — the weighted 7-POINT CHECKLIST (major: change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour = 2 points each; minor: largest diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing/crusting, change in sensation = 1 each) and/or ABCDE — and recognises that a score of 3 or more, or dermoscopy suggesting melanoma, triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12) — Keith scores about 9 (size 2 + shape 2 + colour 2 + diameter ~8 mm 1 + bleeding/oozing 1 + itch 1); clinical concern below that threshold is a matter for judgement and advice, not an NG12 criterion

Examines the lesion IN PERSON (with dermoscopy if able) and performs a wider skin/lymph-node check rather than relying on the patient’s photo; does not skip examination because it’s a video booking — but does not let arranging that look delay a referral the history already justifies

Acts on the NICE NG12 pathway: refers on a suspected cancer pathway for SUSPECTED MELANOMA (7-point checklist ≥3 or dermoscopy suspicion); restates the threshold, tagged NICE NG12 — and does NOT shave/excise it himself or "watch and wait"

Gives sun-safety and secondary-prevention advice WITHOUT shaming (NICE NG34: shade, clothing, hat and sunscreen, tailored to his higher risk), weights the high-risk occupational profile, and advises monitoring other lesions / when to re-present
Hears the bravado as fear, surfaces the workmate’s death and the breadwinner worry gently, and treats the wife’s concern as the reliable signal rather than colluding with "she’s fussing"
Balances honesty with reassurance (many changing moles are benign, but this needs urgent checking), and addresses the guilt about sun exposure supportively

Safety-nets and follows up: explains the suspected cancer pathway timeframe (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral), when to expect contact and what to do if he hears nothing, and what to expect (specialist assessment, likely excision biopsy), what change would warrant sooner review, ensures he attends, documents the lesion description/score, and tracks the result

worked.txt: "I’m really glad your wife pushed you to come, and I’m not going to just tell you it’s nothing from a photo, because that wouldn’t be fair to you. A mole that’s genuinely CHANGED — grown, gone irregular in shape and colour, itched, bled — is exactly the kind we check properly. Not all moles that change are dangerous, but this one has earned a proper look."

"I need to see it in person, not just on a photo — I’ll look at it closely, ideally with a special magnifier, and check your other moles and the glands nearby too. That’s a few minutes and it’s the only way to do this properly. The video’s a good start, but it can’t replace examining you."

"Based on what you’re describing, this meets the criteria for an urgent skin-cancer referral — you’d be seen quickly by a skin specialist, who’ll likely remove it and check it under the microscope, with the aim of an answer within 28 days of the referral. That’s what the NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, says for a changing mole like this. It is NOT me saying it’s cancer; it’s making sure, quickly, and I won’t be cutting it out myself."

"Can I gently ask — has anything made this scary for you? … Your mate, the melanoma that spread. I’m so sorry. That makes complete sense of why ‘it’s nothing’ felt easier to say. And I’d guess part of it is being the one who keeps the roof over everyone’s heads — being ill isn’t something you can picture. That’s exactly why we check now, early, when things are most treatable."

"On the sun — I’m not here to give you a hard time about years on the roof without cream. But going forward, a bit of protection really matters, and I’ll show you what to watch for on your skin. Caught early, skin cancers are very treatable — which is the whole point of moving fast."

"So: I’ll examine it today and get the urgent referral in. If it changes more, bleeds a lot, or you spot another mole doing the same, come back sooner. I’ll write down exactly how it looks now and follow up the result with you. You came in wanting me to say it’s nothing — what I’m doing instead is making sure you find out properly and fast, because that’s what protects you and the family."

f.learning: A CHANGING, irregular, multi-coloured pigmented lesion (especially with itch or bleeding) in a high-risk patient (fair skin, chronic UV exposure, sunburns, many moles) is suspicious for melanoma and must not be reassured away from a photo or a glance. Apply structured assessment — the weighted 7-point checklist (major features: change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour, 2 points each; minor: diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation, 1 each; a score ≥3 triggers referral) and/or ABCDE — examine in person with dermoscopy and a wider skin/node check, and refer on the melanoma suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12; the Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for a diagnosis or all-clear within 28 days); do not excise or "watch and wait" in primary care. The examinable hidden agenda is bravado over fear: a workmate died of melanoma, and as sole earner he can’t face being ill, so he minimises — the wife’s concern is the reliable signal. Surface the fear, treat sun-safety guilt without shaming, balance honesty with reassurance, and complete the suspected cancer pathway referral with documentation and follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG14 (Melanoma: assessment and management, 2015, updated 2022) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG34 (Sunlight exposure: risks and benefits, 2016) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard
knowledge.summary: A pigmented lesion that has grown over 4 months, with an irregular outline, uneven colour, itch and bleeding, scores well above 3 on the weighted 7-point checklist. That meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral for melanoma — whatever the photo looks like.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for melanoma if a suspicious pigmented skin lesion has a weighted 7-point checklist score of 3 or more, or if dermoscopy suggests melanoma. Consider referral for a pigmented or non-pigmented lesion that suggests nodular melanoma.

Major features, 2 points each: change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour. Minor features, 1 point each: largest diameter 7 mm or more, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation. Keith: size 2 + shape 2 + colour 2 + diameter about 8 mm 1 + bleeding 1 + itch 1 = 9.

A photo can support the referral but cannot exclude melanoma. Arrange an in-person look (whole-skin check, regional lymph nodes, dermoscopy if trained) — but do not let that step delay a referral the history already justifies.

Do not shave, biopsy or remove a suspected melanoma in primary care; the specialist team plans complete excision with margins for accurate staging (clinical practice; NICE NG14 covers staging and treatment).
NHS England: people referred on a suspected cancer pathway should have cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days. Tell him when to expect contact and what to do if he hears nothing.

NICE NG34: give clear sun-protection advice (shade, clothing, hat, sunscreen) tailored to risk. Fair skin, sunburns, many moles and outdoor work put him in a higher-risk group; teach self-examination for new or changing lesions.

dg.d: Open question; let him state his wish for reassurance; treated his wife’s concern as information, not fuss.
Self-employed roofer, sole earner, mortgage and children; sun exposure at work.
History against the weighted 7-point checklist; photo used as support only; in-person whole-skin, node and dermoscopy check arranged.
Benign naevus, seborrhoeic keratosis and melanoma considered; did not anchor on “they all change”.
Scored the lesion (9) against the NICE NG12 threshold of 3 and acted on it; did not reassure from a photo.
Told him plainly the lesion needs urgent checking for melanoma, without claiming certainty either way.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral today; no removal in primary care; what to expect explained; sun-safety advice agreed.
Income worry addressed (fit note, self-employed support); risk factors and self-examination covered.
Chase if no contact within a week; bleeding, rapid growth or new lumps in armpit or neck to report; result followed up.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “tell me it’s nothing” and tested it gently, which surfaced the workmate’s death.
Idea (a normal mole, she’s fussing); concern (melanoma like his workmate, not being able to provide); expectation (reassurance).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a workmate died of melanoma that spread; he’s privately frightened it’s the same but, as sole earner, can’t face being ill, so he minimises; guilt about years of no sun protection — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Donnelly, I’m Dr Lee. Can I confirm your date of birth? … Thanks. What would you like to talk about today?
model.why: Identity check and an open question

model.text: Afternoon. My wife’s been on at me about a mole on my back — says it’s bigger and looks different. I think she’s fussing. I’ve got loads of moles and I’m outside all day, they all change a bit. I’ve got a photo. I really just want you to tell me it’s nothing so she’ll stop worrying, and I can get back to the job.
Thank you for coming on — it sounds like she knows your back better than you do. I’ll look at the photo, ask a few questions, and give you an honest answer. Is that all right?
model.why: Treats the wife’s observation as useful and sets an honest agenda

model.text: Go on then.
When did she first notice it changing, and what has changed — size, shape, colour?
model.why: Asks about change, the strongest feature on the checklist

model.text: Four months, maybe. She says it’s bigger. It’s gone a funny shape, and it’s a few colours now — browny, and a black bit.
Has it been itchy, sore, or bled at all?
model.why: Asks about the minor checklist features

model.text: Itches now and then. It bled once, a little, when I caught it.
Can you hold the photo up to the camera? … Thank you. How big would you say it is — if you had a ruler?
model.why: Uses the photo to support, not replace, the assessment

model.text: About eight millimetres, I reckon.
And your skin in general — do you burn easily? Many sunburns over the years? Do you use sun cream at work?
Fair as anything. Burnt loads as a kid and on the roofs. Never bothered with cream, to be honest.
You said you want me to tell you it’s nothing. Has any part of you wondered whether it might be something?
(Pause.) A lad I worked with — he had a melanoma. It spread everywhere. That was a couple of years back. I try not to think about it.
I’m really sorry. That must have been awful, and it makes complete sense that this has been sitting at the back of your mind.
model.why: Acknowledges the fear behind the minimising

model.text: And I’m self-employed. No work, no money. Mortgage, kids. I can’t be ill.
Thank you for telling me. That’s a lot of pressure. Let’s make a plan that deals with this properly and quickly — that’s the best protection for your family too.
model.why: Names the breadwinner pressure and ties the plan to it

model.text: I’ll be honest with you. Most changing moles turn out not to be cancer. But this one has grown, changed shape and colour, is over seven millimetres, itches and has bled. We use a checklist for moles, and yours scores well above the level where the guidance says it should be seen urgently by a skin specialist to check for melanoma.
model.why: Applies the 7-point checklist and states the NICE NG12 threshold plainly

model.text: So you think it is one.

I can’t tell from a photo, and neither could anyone. What I can say is that it needs checking quickly. If it is a melanoma, finding it at this stage — on the skin, before it’s spread — is exactly when treatment works best. Your wife did you a real favour.
model.why: Balances honesty with hope and credits the wife

model.text: Right. (Pause.) Okay.

Here’s the plan. I’m making an urgent suspected cancer referral to dermatology today. The aim is that you’ll know one way or the other within 28 days. I’d also like to see you in person in the next day or two to look at it properly, check the rest of your skin and feel for glands — but the referral goes today regardless.
model.why: Refers today on the suspected cancer pathway and arranges an in-person skin and node check

model.text: What will they do?

Usually they look at it under a special magnifier, and if it needs to come off they’ll remove it under local anaesthetic and send it to the lab. Please don’t try to deal with it yourself or let anyone else remove it — it needs to be done properly by them.
model.why: Explains what to expect and avoids primary-care removal

model.text: And the time off?

Most appointments are short, and a small removal usually means a short break from heavy work. If you do need time off, there’s help for self-employed people, and I can give you a fit note. We’ll deal with that as it comes.
And for the future — no lecture — but on the roofs, a hat, a shirt with sleeves and sun cream on the bits that are out will make a real difference. Would you be up for that?
model.why: Sun-safety advice without blame, with his agreement

model.text: Yeah. She’ll make sure I do.

If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. If it bleeds a lot, grows quickly, or you find a new lump in your armpit or neck, get in touch sooner. Can you tell me back what’s happening next?
Referral today, you see me in a couple of days, the hospital should call within a week — if not, I ring you. And sun cream.
Perfect. I’ll follow up the result with you. Would it help if your wife joined next time?
model.why: Offers to include the family and commits to follow-up

model.text: Maybe. Thanks, doc.

social.t: No sick pay, a mortgage and children. The thought of cancer is the thought of not providing, which drives the minimising and could lead to missed appointments.
Roofing means chronic sun exposure. Practical protection on site (hat, sleeves, shade, sunscreen) is more useful than general advice.

legal.t: Self-employed people cannot get Statutory Sick Pay. New Style ESA may apply depending on National Insurance contributions, and Universal Credit depending on household income. A fit note can be issued if he needs time off.
HSE publishes sun-protection advice for outdoor workers; as self-employed, he is responsible for his own protection on site.

professional.t: Video and photos cannot exclude melanoma. Refer on the history and arrange an in-person examination; document the lesion description and checklist score (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Tell him when to expect contact and to ring if he hears nothing; the practice should track the referral and the result.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support for financial and emotional support if needed; Melanoma Focus for patient information; British Association of Dermatologists sun-awareness resources.

redFlags: Change in size, shape or colour of a pigmented lesion — major checklist features
Diameter 7 mm or more, itch, bleeding or inflammation — minor features
New lumps in the armpit or neck; a raised, firm, fast-growing lesion (nodular melanoma)
psychosocial: Workmate died of melanoma a couple of years ago
Self-employed sole earner — mortgage and children
Guilt about years without sun protection
ice: Idea: “It’s just one of my moles — they all change.”
Concern: melanoma like his workmate; not being able to provide
Expectation: reassurance so his wife stops worrying

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest and specific: “This mole has grown, changed shape and colour, is over seven millimetres, itches and has bled. That’s enough to need an urgent specialist check for melanoma — most turn out not to be, but we must be sure.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of an ordinary mole as a car parked in the same spot for years. This one has been moving and changing colour. That doesn’t mean it’s dangerous, but it means someone expert needs to look at it quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your workmate, I can see why you’d rather not think about it. Acting quickly now is the best way to protect you and your family.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around his work — short appointments, fit note if needed, self-employed income support; invite his wife to the next appointment if he wishes.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to dermatology today (NICE NG12: score 3 or more)
In-person whole-skin, node and dermoscopy check within a day or two
No removal in primary care; sun protection at work agreed
safetyNet: Ring if no contact from the hospital within a week
Report heavy bleeding, rapid growth or new lumps in the armpit or neck

pitfalls.intro: The clinical answer here is simple — the checklist score makes the referral. The station is failed on being talked out of it by a patient who wants reassurance, and on missing the fear he brings.

items.fail: Reassuring from the photo, or booking a review in a few months.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG12: refer if the weighted 7-point checklist score is 3 or more.
items.fix: Score it aloud — change in size, shape and colour, 8 mm, itch, bleeding — and refer today.

items.fail: Offering to shave or remove it at the surgery.
items.why: Partial or unplanned removal of a melanoma compromises diagnosis and staging.
items.fix: “The specialist team will remove it properly and send it to the lab.”

items.fail: Relying on the video and never arranging an in-person look.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information.” A whole-skin check and node examination are part of the assessment.
items.fix: Refer today on the history, and see him in person within a day or two.

items.fail: Agreeing that his wife is fussing.
items.why: Colluding with minimising undermines the referral he needs to accept.
items.fix: “She’s noticed something important — she’s done you a favour.”

items.fail: Missing the workmate and the money worry.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s concerns.” Without them, the risk of non-attendance stays hidden.
items.fix: “Has any part of you wondered if it might be something?” Then address income directly.

items.fail: No plan for what happens if the hospital doesn’t call.
items.why: Referrals get lost; safety-netting must cover the system as well as symptoms.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it.” Then teach-back.

timeMap.d: He wants reassurance for his wife. Take her observation seriously and promise an honest answer, not a quick one.
Change in size, shape and colour; diameter; itch, bleeding, inflammation; skin type, sunburns, sun protection, number of moles. Use the photo as support.
The workmate who died of melanoma; sole earner, self-employed. Let the bravado drop before you explain.
Checklist score well above 3: suspected cancer pathway referral today (NICE NG12). In-person skin and node check. No removal in primary care. Sun safety without blame. Income support.
Chase if no contact within a week; bleeding, rapid growth or new lumps to report. Teach-back. Offer to include his wife.

wordPics.fail: Looks at the photo and says it looks like an ordinary mole; or books a routine review in a few months; or offers to remove it at the surgery; never asks about change, itch or bleeding; misses the workmate and the money worry.
wordPics.pass: Takes a structured history, recognises a suspicious changing lesion, makes a suspected cancer pathway referral, arranges an in-person check and gives sun-safety advice and a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: scores the checklist aloud against the NICE NG12 threshold; credits his wife; surfaces the workmate and his fears as a provider; balances honesty with the reason for hope; covers income support and a chase-up plan; closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “From the photo it looks like a normal mole — keep an eye on it.”
avoid.instead: “A photo can’t rule this out, and the changes you describe mean it needs urgent checking.”
avoid.why: Reassurance from a photo in a lesion scoring 9 is the dangerous fail here.

avoid.dont: “You really should have been wearing sun cream all these years.”
avoid.instead: “From now on, a hat, sleeves and sun cream on the roofs will make a real difference.”
avoid.why: Blame adds to the guilt he already carries and shuts the conversation down.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably cancer, but they can treat it.”
avoid.instead: “Most changing moles aren’t cancer — but this one needs checking quickly to be sure.”
avoid.why: Overstating certainty either way is inaccurate and frightening.

SCA_MODELS.why: Refers today on the suspected cancer pathway and arranges an in-person skin and node check

SCA_MODELS.text: What will they do?

Usually they look at it under a special magnifier, and if it needs to come off they’ll remove it under local anaesthetic and send it to the lab. Please don’t try to deal with it yourself or let anyone else remove it — it needs to be done properly by them.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains what to expect and avoids primary-care removal

SCA_MODELS.text: And the time off?

Most appointments are short, and a small removal usually means a short break from heavy work. If you do need time off, there’s help for self-employed people, and I can give you a fit note. We’ll deal with that as it comes.
And for the future — no lecture — but on the roofs, a hat, a shirt with sleeves and sun cream on the bits that are out will make a real difference. Would you be up for that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Sun-safety advice without blame, with his agreement

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. She’ll make sure I do.

If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it. If it bleeds a lot, grows quickly, or you find a new lump in your armpit or neck, get in touch sooner. Can you tell me back what’s happening next?
Referral today, you see me in a couple of days, the hospital should call within a week — if not, I ring you. And sun cream.
Perfect. I’ll follow up the result with you. Would it help if your wife joined next time?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers to include the family and commits to follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. Thanks, doc.

SCA_STEM.name: Keith Donnelly
SCA_STEM.recent: No previous skin consultations on record. Occupation: roofer (self-employed).
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment booked at his wife’s request: “a mole on my back that’s changed”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG14 (Melanoma: assessment and management, 2015, updated 2022) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG34 (Sunlight exposure: risks and benefits, 2016) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A pigmented lesion that has grown over 4 months, with an irregular outline, uneven colour, itch and bleeding, scores well above 3 on the weighted 7-point checklist. That meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway referral for melanoma — whatever the photo looks like.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer using a suspected cancer pathway referral for melanoma if a suspicious pigmented skin lesion has a weighted 7-point checklist score of 3 or more, or if dermoscopy suggests melanoma. Consider referral for a pigmented or non-pigmented lesion that suggests nodular melanoma.

Major features, 2 points each: change in size, irregular shape, irregular colour. Minor features, 1 point each: largest diameter 7 mm or more, inflammation, oozing, change in sensation. Keith: size 2 + shape 2 + colour 2 + diameter about 8 mm 1 + bleeding 1 + itch 1 = 9.

A photo can support the referral but cannot exclude melanoma. Arrange an in-person look (whole-skin check, regional lymph nodes, dermoscopy if trained) — but do not let that step delay a referral the history already justifies.

Do not shave, biopsy or remove a suspected melanoma in primary care; the specialist team plans complete excision with margins for accurate staging (clinical practice; NICE NG14 covers staging and treatment).
NHS England: people referred on a suspected cancer pathway should have cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days. Tell him when to expect contact and what to do if he hears nothing.

NICE NG34: give clear sun-protection advice (shade, clothing, hat, sunscreen) tailored to risk. Fair skin, sunburns, many moles and outdoor work put him in a higher-risk group; teach self-examination for new or changing lesions.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him state his wish for reassurance; treated his wife’s concern as information, not fuss.
Self-employed roofer, sole earner, mortgage and children; sun exposure at work.
Picked up “tell me it’s nothing” and tested it gently, which surfaced the workmate’s death.
Idea (a normal mole, she’s fussing); concern (melanoma like his workmate, not being able to provide); expectation (reassurance).
History against the weighted 7-point checklist; photo used as support only; in-person whole-skin, node and dermoscopy check arranged.
Benign naevus, seborrhoeic keratosis and melanoma considered; did not anchor on “they all change”.
Scored the lesion (9) against the NICE NG12 threshold of 3 and acted on it; did not reassure from a photo.
Told him plainly the lesion needs urgent checking for melanoma, without claiming certainty either way.
Suspected cancer pathway referral today; no removal in primary care; what to expect explained; sun-safety advice agreed.
Income worry addressed (fit note, self-employed support); risk factors and self-examination covered.
Chase if no contact within a week; bleeding, rapid growth or new lumps in armpit or neck to report; result followed up.

social.t: No sick pay, a mortgage and children. The thought of cancer is the thought of not providing, which drives the minimising and could lead to missed appointments.
Roofing means chronic sun exposure. Practical protection on site (hat, sleeves, shade, sunscreen) is more useful than general advice.

legal.t: Self-employed people cannot get Statutory Sick Pay. New Style ESA may apply depending on National Insurance contributions, and Universal Credit depending on household income. A fit note can be issued if he needs time off.
HSE publishes sun-protection advice for outdoor workers; as self-employed, he is responsible for his own protection on site.

professional.t: Video and photos cannot exclude melanoma. Refer on the history and arrange an in-person examination; document the lesion description and checklist score (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Tell him when to expect contact and to ring if he hears nothing; the practice should track the referral and the result.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support for financial and emotional support if needed; Melanoma Focus for patient information; British Association of Dermatologists sun-awareness resources.

redFlags: Change in size, shape or colour of a pigmented lesion — major checklist features
Diameter 7 mm or more, itch, bleeding or inflammation — minor features
New lumps in the armpit or neck; a raised, firm, fast-growing lesion (nodular melanoma)
psychosocial: Workmate died of melanoma a couple of years ago
Self-employed sole earner — mortgage and children
Guilt about years without sun protection
ice: Idea: “It’s just one of my moles — they all change.”
Concern: melanoma like his workmate; not being able to provide
Expectation: reassurance so his wife stops worrying

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest and specific: “This mole has grown, changed shape and colour, is over seven millimetres, itches and has bled. That’s enough to need an urgent specialist check for melanoma — most turn out not to be, but we must be sure.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of an ordinary mole as a car parked in the same spot for years. This one has been moving and changing colour. That doesn’t mean it’s dangerous, but it means someone expert needs to look at it quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your workmate, I can see why you’d rather not think about it. Acting quickly now is the best way to protect you and your family.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around his work — short appointments, fit note if needed, self-employed income support; invite his wife to the next appointment if he wishes.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway referral to dermatology today (NICE NG12: score 3 or more)
In-person whole-skin, node and dermoscopy check within a day or two
No removal in primary care; sun protection at work agreed
safetyNet: Ring if no contact from the hospital within a week
Report heavy bleeding, rapid growth or new lumps in the armpit or neck

SCA_LINKS.s: Management protocol · sun damage and protection

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical answer here is simple — the checklist score makes the referral. The station is failed on being talked out of it by a patient who wants reassurance, and on missing the fear he brings.

items.fail: Reassuring from the photo, or booking a review in a few months.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG12: refer if the weighted 7-point checklist score is 3 or more.
items.fix: Score it aloud — change in size, shape and colour, 8 mm, itch, bleeding — and refer today.

items.fail: Offering to shave or remove it at the surgery.
items.why: Partial or unplanned removal of a melanoma compromises diagnosis and staging.
items.fix: “The specialist team will remove it properly and send it to the lab.”

items.fail: Relying on the video and never arranging an in-person look.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information.” A whole-skin check and node examination are part of the assessment.
items.fix: Refer today on the history, and see him in person within a day or two.

items.fail: Agreeing that his wife is fussing.
items.why: Colluding with minimising undermines the referral he needs to accept.
items.fix: “She’s noticed something important — she’s done you a favour.”

items.fail: Missing the workmate and the money worry.
items.why: “Does not identify the patient’s concerns.” Without them, the risk of non-attendance stays hidden.
items.fix: “Has any part of you wondered if it might be something?” Then address income directly.

items.fail: No plan for what happens if the hospital doesn’t call.
items.why: Referrals get lost; safety-netting must cover the system as well as symptoms.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it.” Then teach-back.
